title: Vayikra: offering means nearness
hookLine: the word for offering comes from the root "to come near"

cards: Say sacrifice, and loss is close behind: a parent who sacrifices sleep, a soldier who sacrifices everything, a chess player who sacrifices a piece. In everyday speech, a sacrifice is mostly about what you lose.
Leviticus is full of what English Bibles call offerings and sacrifices: animals, grain, oil, wine. Read it with only the English, and it can sound like a book about giving things up.
The Hebrew word underneath says something else entirely.

teach.b: The word is korban, from the Hebrew root kuf, resh, bet: to be near, to come close. The same root gives karov, near, which in modern Hebrew also means a relative, someone close to you.
And the verb for bringing an offering, hikriv, literally means to bring near.

So the book's second verse, "When any man of you bringeth an offering unto the LORD," could be heard as: when one of you brings something near to God. In the language itself, a korban isn't about losing something.
It's about closing a distance. Some Hasidic teachers noticed the odd word order in the Hebrew of that verse, which can be read: when a person brings near, of yourselves, an offering.

teach.h: THE REAL OFFERING IS THE SELF.
teach.b: The real offering, they said, is the self. Then history made the question urgent. When the Second Temple was destroyed, the offerings stopped.
How do you come near without an altar?
The prophet Hosea had already given a phrase for it: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips."
The Talmud records the teaching that the daily prayers stand in place of the daily offerings, and traditional prayer books still include passages about the offerings in the morning service.
In that teaching, what the altar did, closing a distance, is now done with words.

how: Jewish tradition teaches that the daily prayers correspond to the daily Temple offerings, and traditional prayer books include readings about the offerings, called korbanot, in the morning service.

o: an offering: a bringing near to God
an altar: the stone where gifts burn
a loss: something given up for good

games.q: the Second Temple has just been destroyed, and there's no altar left. how do people come near to God now?
o: they don't, until a new Temple is built.
through prayer: the offering of our lips.
by building altars in every town.
games.why: the rabbis taught that prayer stands in place of the offerings, as Hosea put it: so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips.

practice: Think of something you've drifted from: a person you haven't called, a practice you used to keep, a part of yourself you've ignored, or, if you pray, God.
Don't try to close the whole distance; just picture one step nearer, a text, a page, a minute. Stay near it for a while, and notice what that one step gives.

wordCard.voice: Korban. An offering, from the root meaning to come near. Not a giving up, but a bringing close.

orig.note: Hebrew: an offering, from the root to come near.
